brave.snippet:
Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit ... Eric Holmes was convicted by an Indiana jury in 1992 of two counts of murder, attempted murder, robbery, and conspiracy to commit robbery, stemming from an incident at a restaurant. During sentencing, the jury could not unanimously recommend the death penalty, so the trial judge, as allowed by Indiana law at the time, found aggravating circumstances and imposed a death sentence.
Holmes then filed a second federal habeas petition in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, claiming the Indiana Supreme Court’s decision violated his Fourteenth Amendment rights to equal protection. The district court dismissed the petition as “second or successive,” lacking jurisdiction. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit disagreed with the district court’s procedural ruling, finding Holmes’s equal protection claim was not “second or successive” because it was not ripe during his first petition.
However, the court affirmed the dismissal on the merits, holding the Indiana Supreme Court had a rational basis for treating Holmes differently, since his jury had not reached a unanimous recommendation, and thus there was no Equal Protection violation. octen.snippet:
No habeas relief for alleged errors in capital case
Eric D. Holmes v. Ron Neal, 7th Circuit Court of Appeals Nos. 04-3549, 06-2905, and 14-3359, 3/22/16
Holmes claims various errors in his capital murder case merit habeas relief, but the 7th Circuit doesn’t agree.
Holmes’s primary claims involve unanticipated testimony by a sheriff’s deputy during the guilt phase of his trial and various errors during the penalty phase. As to the guilt phase error, Holmes’s attorney was given an overnight recess to deal with the testimony, and in any event Holmes wasn’t significantly harmed by the testimony. (Slip op. at 6). As to the penalty phase errors, the improper closing argument to the jury by the prosecutor was handled appropriately by the trial court’s striking the remarks from the record (and in any event the jury’s verdict on penalty was only advisory) and the claim Holmes’s lawyer failed to advance certain claims at sentencing are belied by the record, which shows counsel made the essential points Holmes now says he failed to present. (Slip op. at 5-6, 7-8).
Holmes also has a claim that he is not sufficiently mentally competent to be executed under Atkins v. Virginia, 536 U.S. 304 (2002), but that claim is premature because the state has not yet set an execution date and thus there’s not yet been a hearing to determine his competence.

parallel.title: A later habeas petition cleared one barrier but failed on equal protection | US Law Explained
parallel.snippet:
Eric D. Holmes challenged unequal treatment in Indiana's handling of death sentences after changes to its capital-sentencing law. The Seventh Circuit concluded that his later federal habeas petition was not barred as an unauthorized second or successive petition. It nevertheless affirmed denial of relief because his equal-protection claim failed. The October 15, 2026 decision therefore resolved two distinct questions in different ways: the court could entertain this claim, but the claim did not warrant relief. It did not order a new sentencing hearing or establish a later execution date. [1]

The Court’s Holding

The Seventh Circuit held that Holmes’s 2005 petition was not “second or successive” within the meaning of § 2244(b). His equal-protection claim did not become ripe until the Indiana Supreme Court denied him permission in 2005 to pursue another state post-conviction petition. Because that allegedly discriminatory judicial action occurred after Holmes filed his first federal petition, AEDPA’s restrictions on second or successive petitions did not bar the later claim.
The court nevertheless affirmed because Holmes’s equal-protection claim failed on the merits. Saylor and the other proposed comparators had received death sentences despite unanimous jury recommendations against death, a procedure expressly prohibited by Indiana’s amended statute. Holmes’s jury, by contrast, reached no sentencing recommendation, and the statute continued to permit judicial sentencing after a jury deadlock. The Indiana Supreme Court also had a rational basis for declining to apply the amended special-verdict requirement retroactively: Holmes’s guilt-phase verdicts necessarily established beyond a reasonable doubt the charged aggravators of multiple murders and murder during a robbery. The court assumed without deciding that a class-of-one equal-protection challenge could reach state judicial action.
Judge Jackson-Akiwumi concurred in the judgment. She agreed that the petition was not successive and that circuit precedent required rejection of the equal-protection claim, but emphasized serious concerns about Indiana’s capital-sentencing procedure, the absence of penalty-phase jury findings on special verdict forms, and the Indiana Supreme Court’s differing treatment of Holmes and other capital defendants.

* A later-in-time habeas petition is not necessarily “second or successive” when its claim could not have ripened before adjudication of the first petition.

**Court:** U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
**Docket Number:** 23-2890
**Date Decided:** October 15, 2026
Justia Opinion Summary
Eric Holmes was convicted by an Indiana jury in 1992 of two counts of murder, attempted murder, robbery, and conspiracy to commit robbery, stemming from an incide
nt at a restaurant.
During sentencing, the jury could not unanimously recommend the death penalty, so the trial judge, as allowed by Indiana law at the time, found aggravating circumstances and imposed a death sentence.
Holmes exhausted his direct appeals and post-conviction relief in state court, then filed a federal habeas corpus petition.
...
Holmes then
filed a second federal habeas petition in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, claiming the Indiana Supreme Court’s decision violated his Fourteenth Amendment rights to equal protection.
The district court dismissed the petition as “second or successive,” lacking jurisdiction.
On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit disagreed with the district court’s procedural ruling, finding Holmes’s equal protection claim was not “second or successive” bec
ause it was not ripe during his first petition.
However, the court affirmed the dismissal on the merits, holding the Indiana Supreme Court had a rational basis for treating Holmes differently, since his jury had not reached a unanimous recommendation, and thus there was no Equal Protection violation.

Holmes’s primary claims involve unanticipated testimony by a sheriff’s deputy during the guilt phase of his trial and various errors during the penalty phase.
